newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-ITALY LOOKING GOOD FOR 1998 WORLD CUP.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ITALY LOOKING GOOD FOR 1998 WORLD CUP.

text.p: Even a Hollywood scriptwriter would have found it difficult to come up with a better screenplay than the story of Italy's 3-0 World Cup win against Moldova in Trieste on Saturday.
Italian coach Cesare Maldini was cast in the role of returning local hero, back in his native town as coach to the country's footballing pride.

His son Paolo, in the unusual role of sharpshooter, upheld family honour and rewarded the 25,000-strong Trieste crowd's warm support with an opening goal of breathtaking class which set up the Italian victory.
Cast in the role of newcomer, Juventus striker Christian Vieri made a dream debut scoring Italy's 1,000th goal in international soccer.
All in all, it was a very successful night for Italy who now lead World Cup qualifying group two with 12 points, three clear of second-placed England.
Little wonder, then, that coach Maldini expressed himself afterwards as "not just satisfied, but very satisfied".
The Italian squad, though, will not lose much time celebrating what was, after all, an entirely predictable win against modest opponents.

On Wednesday, Italy travel to Poland for what is expected to be a much more difficult qualifier in Chorzow. Chelsea midfielder Roberto Di Matteo has no doubt but that Poland will prove much tougher rivals than Moldova.
"On paper and I imagine on the pitch, the game against Poland will be a lot harder. I saw them against England at Wembley and they're a good side," he said.
Teammate Stefano Eranio, who came on as a second half substitute for Angelo Di Livio, agreed.
"Poland will be a difficult side to play against but if we go there and play with the same attitude that we showed tonight, then things should go well."
Although Cesare Maldini intends to wait and assess how his players have come out of the Moldova game before naming his side to face Poland, there are no real doubts about his selection.
Unlike his controversial predecessor Arrigo Sacchi, the man he replaced last December, Maldini is most unlikely to want to alter a winning side.
The injury enforced replacement of Lazio defender Alessandro Nesta by Parma's Fabio Cannavaro may be the only change from the side which started against Moldova.
Gianfranco Zola and Vieri will again lead the attack, with Demetrio Albertini, Roberto Di Matteo, Dino Baggio and Angelo Di Livio again in midfield.
One observer much impressed by Italy's peformance in Trieste on Saturday night was Ryszard Kulesza, deputy President of the Polish Football Federation:
"On Wednesday it'll be a very difficult game for us because we don't have the great class players of former times, players like Zibi Boniek," he said.
"Now we have a medium level side with no stars but some useful players with only (Marek) Citko being above average."
